title: Starting Your Practice: Brokerage Models, Teams & Business Planning
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: A salesperson receives 1099 income from her brokerage. For purposes of the Real Estate Law's supervision requirements, she is treated as:
options: An independent principal responsible only to herself
The employee of her responsible broker
A co-broker with shared liability
An unsupervised contractor
rationales: Tax classification does not relieve the broker of supervision duties or the salesperson of working under them.
Correct. A salesperson may be an independent contractor for tax purposes while being treated as the broker's employee for supervision and accountability — both are true simultaneously.
Salespersons do not hold co-broker status.
All licensed activity by a salesperson is subject to broker supervision.

questions.stem: In a cap-based commission model, the 'cap' refers to:
options: The maximum commission a client may be charged
A cumulative amount paid to the brokerage in a year, after which the agent's split improves
The largest transaction size the brokerage will accept
A limit on the agent's annual earnings
rationales: Commissions charged to clients are always negotiable and are not capped by brokerage models.
Correct. Once the agent has paid the brokerage the cap amount within the anniversary year, the split typically improves, often to 100%.
Caps concern compensation structure, not transaction size limits.
A cap raises an agent's earnings after it is met; it does not limit them.

questions.stem: An agent expects 6 transactions at $19,500 gross commission per side. Brokerage A offers a 60/40 split with a $395 per-transaction fee and no desk fee. The agent's annual net from Brokerage A is:
rationales: $117,000 is total gross commission for six sides before any split.
$70,200 applies the 60% split but omits the per-transaction fees.
$63,180 applies a 54% split, which is not the stated arrangement.

questions.stem: A fixed monthly desk fee is MOST damaging to an agent's economics when:
options: Transaction volume is high
Transaction volume is low
The market is appreciating
The agent works on a team
rationales: At high volume the fixed fee is spread across many closings and its per-transaction impact shrinks.
Correct. A fixed fee is owed whether or not the agent closes anything, so it hurts most at low volume — exactly when a new agent can least absorb it.
Market direction does not change the fixed nature of the fee.
Team membership does not alter how a fixed fee interacts with volume.

questions.stem: A California salesperson team wishes to advertise under a team name. The name must generally:
options: Be registered as a fictitious business name by the salesperson
Include a team member's surname plus a term such as 'team,' 'group,' or 'associates'
Be approved by the local association of Realtors
Include the word 'Realty' to signal professionalism
rationales: Salespersons do not obtain their own fictitious business name licensing; that is a broker function.

Correct. A team name must generally include a team member's surname together with a term like team, group, or associates, must not imply an independent brokerage, and advertising must identify the responsible broker.
Association approval is not the legal requirement.
Terms suggesting an independent brokerage — like 'Realty' — are precisely what the rule guards against.

questions.stem: A team sign displays only the team name and a phone number, with no mention of the brokerage. This creates a risk of:
options: A blind ad, because it conceals that the advertiser is a licensee acting through a broker
A RESPA violation
A trust fund violation
An antitrust violation
rationales: Correct. Advertising that hides the licensee's status and the responsible broker is a blind ad and is prohibited; team advertising must identify the broker.
RESPA governs settlement service referrals and kickbacks, not signage.
Trust fund rules govern client money, not advertising.
Antitrust concerns price-fixing and market allocation, not sign content.

questions.stem: An agent needs to earn $60,000. Median price is $540,000, she earns a 2.5% side, and her split is 70/30 in her favor. She needs approximately:
options: 5 transactions
7 transactions
9 transactions
4 transactions
rationales: 5 transactions would yield about $47,250, short of the goal.
Correct. $540,000 × 0.025 = $13,500 gross per side; × 0.70 = $9,450 to the agent; $60,000 ÷ $9,450 = 6.35, so 7 transactions.
9 transactions would substantially exceed the target.
4 transactions would yield about $37,800.

questions.stem: Because a salesperson receives 1099 income with no withholding, the most important financial habit in year one is to:
options: Maximize deductions by delaying expense tracking until tax season
Set aside a portion of every commission for taxes and pay quarterly estimates
Wait until the first tax return to determine liability
Treat all commission income as spendable
rationales: Delaying expense tracking loses deductions and makes reconstruction difficult.
Correct. Nothing is withheld from commission checks, so the agent must reserve roughly 25–35% for income and self-employment tax and make quarterly estimated payments.
Waiting until filing produces a liability the agent has not reserved for.
Treating gross commission as spendable income is the classic first-year mistake.

questions.stem: Errors and omissions insurance generally does NOT cover:
options: An alleged failure to disclose a known material fact
A clerical error in preparing a contract
Commingling or misappropriation of trust funds
A negligence claim arising from a showing
rationales: Disclosure claims are a core reason E&O exists.
Errors in document preparation are within typical coverage.
Correct. E&O excludes intentional wrongdoing, fraud, and trust fund misappropriation — there is no insurance product for taking client money.
Negligence claims arising from professional services are typically covered.

questions.stem: For a brand-new licensee, the factor most predictive of remaining in the business past year two is:
options: Securing the highest available commission split
Having six to twelve months of living expenses in reserve
Joining the largest national brand
Buying online portal leads immediately
rationales: A high split on zero closings is worth nothing.
Correct. Commissions arrive months after work begins, and running out of money before the pipeline matures is the most common reason new agents leave.
Brand size does not address the cash flow gap.
Purchased leads add cost during the period when cash is scarcest.

questions.stem: When interviewing brokerages, the question most valuable to a new licensee is:
options: What is your commission split?
Who reviews my first purchase contract, and who do I call on a Sunday?
How many agents work here?
What is your market share?
rationales: Split matters, but it is secondary to competence and liability protection in year one.
Correct. Supervision quality is both the fastest route to competence and a liability shield, and it is the question new agents most often fail to ask.
Headcount says little about the support an individual agent receives.
Brokerage market share does not translate into support for a new licensee.

questions.stem: A franchise fee in a national brand brokerage is typically taken:
options: From the agent's share after the broker split
Off the top of the commission before the broker/agent split
Only from the broker's share
Annually as a flat membership charge
rationales: Taking it after the split would understate its effect on the agent.
Correct. A franchise fee is commonly deducted off the top before the split, which is why agents must model it explicitly when comparing offers.
The fee reduces the pool both parties share, not only the broker's portion.
Franchise fees are typically transaction-based rather than a flat annual charge.

questions.stem: A new agent joins a team that supplies leads and takes 50% of the agent's side on team-generated business. The primary trade-off being accepted is:
options: Higher compensation for less work
Lower per-transaction income in exchange for lead flow, systems, and supervision
Freedom from broker supervision
Exemption from team advertising rules
rationales: Team splits reduce per-transaction income; the benefit lies elsewhere.
Correct. The agent trades a smaller share for leads before they can generate their own, established systems, and experienced review of their work — often the fastest route to competence.
Team members remain fully subject to the responsible broker's supervision.
Team advertising rules apply regardless of the compensation arrangement.

questions.stem: Which expense is most commonly omitted from a new agent's first-year budget?
options: MLS and association dues
Six to twelve months of personal living expenses
Business cards
A lockbox key
rationales: Dues are a known, recurring line most agents anticipate.
Correct. New agents routinely budget business costs and omit the personal runway needed to survive the four to six month gap before the first commission arrives.
Marketing materials are typically anticipated.
Lockbox access is a small, expected cost.

questions.stem: A new agent is unsure how to complete an unfamiliar contract provision. The correct action is to:
options: Draft language that captures the parties' intent
Ask the responsible broker before completing it
Copy language from a contract in another transaction
Leave it blank and address it at closing
rationales: Drafting custom legal language is the unauthorized practice of law.
Correct. Broker supervision exists for exactly this, and asking is both the competent and the protected course.
Borrowing language from an unrelated transaction risks importing terms that do not fit and still amounts to drafting.
Leaving material terms blank creates ambiguity and potential unenforceability.

questions.stem: An agent closes 2 transactions in year one at $19,500 per side. Brokerage A: 60/40 split, $395 per transaction, no desk fee. Brokerage B: 80/20 split, $295 per transaction, $800 monthly desk fee. Which nets more, and why?
options: Brokerage A, because $9,600 in annual desk fees outweighs B's better split at this volume
Brokerage B, because a higher split always wins
The two are identical at every volume
Brokerage B, because per-transaction fees matter more than desk fees
rationales: Correct. A: ($19,500 × 0.60 − $395) × 2 = $22,610. B: ($19,500 × 0.80 − $295) × 2 − $9,600 = $30,610 − $9,600 = $21,010. A nets $1,600 more, because fixed fees are owed regardless of production and dominate at low volume.
A higher split only wins once volume is sufficient to absorb the fixed costs; at two transactions it does not.
The structures diverge at every volume; which one leads depends on transaction count.
Here the $9,600 in desk fees dwarfs the $200 per-transaction difference — the fixed cost is what decides it.

questions.stem: Working backward from an income goal, the most useful final output of a business plan is:
options: A target gross commission income figure
A daily or weekly activity count the agent can schedule
A list of desired brokerages
A projected market appreciation rate
rationales: An income target is the starting input, not something the agent can act on directly.
Correct. Converting the income goal into transactions, then into conversations, produces a schedulable daily activity — and consistent activity, not knowledge, is what new agents most often lack.
Brokerage selection is a separate decision.
Appreciation is outside the agent's control and does not drive daily behavior.

questions.stem: The habit that most reduces an agent's long-term liability exposure is:
options: Carrying higher E&O limits
Confirming every material conversation in writing the same day
Working only with referred clients
Avoiding older properties
rationales: Higher limits pay claims; they do not prevent them.
Correct. A written record created contemporaneously is the single most effective protection, because most disputes turn on what was said and when.
Referred clients sue too, and limiting the client base is not a risk strategy.
Property age does not determine liability; disclosure practice does.
